summary: Adds three properties to vCard 4.0: place of birth, place of death and date of death. The base vCard format already had date of birth.

plainLanguage.summary: A digital contact card could already record birthdays. This adds places of birth and death and a death date, useful for things like family-history records.

subtitle: Three new vCard 4.0 properties for recording where someone was born, where they died, and when they died.

tldr.problem: The base vCard 4.0 format already had a property for date of birth, but no way to record place of birth, place of death or date of death.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three properties, BIRTHPLACE, DEATHPLACE and DEATHDATE, each with a value type, a cardinality of at most one, allowed parameters and an ABNF definition, in the same style as the base specification.
tldr.outcome: The properties are registered in the IANA vCard Properties registry, so any vCard 4.0 implementation can use them.

today: RFC 6474 is a Proposed Standard from December 2011. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on RFC 6350.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6474 extends vCard 4.0, the contact-card format defined in RFC 6350. That base specification defines a large number of properties, including date of birth. This document adds three more: BIRTHPLACE, DEATHPLACE and DEATHDATE.

The Acknowledgements section says the properties originated in a draft version of RFC 6350, whose authors Simon Perreault and Pete Resnick are thanked.
sections.plainLanguage: A contact card is like a small form with boxes for a person's details. This RFC adds three new boxes to the form.

sections.title: Terminology and Notation
sections.content:
The key words MUST, SHOULD, MAY and the others are used as described in RFC 2119. Syntax is written in augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) as described in RFC 5234, and is specified the same way as in the base vCard specification, RFC 6350.

Each property is described with the same template as the base format: property name, purpose, value type, cardinality, allowed parameters, description, format definition and examples.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC fills in each new box using the same form layout as the old ones, so the new boxes look familiar.

sections.title: BIRTHPLACE and DEATHPLACE
sections.content:
BIRTHPLACE specifies the place of birth of the object the vCard represents. DEATHPLACE does the same for the place of death. They are defined identically apart from the name.

The value is a single text value by default, or a single URI value. The VALUE parameter says which (text or uri), and the value type and the VALUE parameter MUST match. Cardinality is *1, so each property may appear at most once. Allowed parameters are VALUE and LANGUAGE, plus altid and any other parameter through the ABNF.

A URI value can point to a description of the place or use the geo: scheme to give coordinates.
sections.plainLanguage: You can write the place as plain words, like a hospital name, or as a link or map coordinates that point to it.

sections.title: DEATHDATE
sections.content:
DEATHDATE specifies the date of death. Its default value type is a single date-and-or-time value, and it can be reset to a single text value with VALUE=text. Cardinality is *1. Allowed parameters are VALUE, CALSCALE and LANGUAGE.

CALSCALE can only be present when the value is a date-and-or-time value that actually contains a date or date-time. LANGUAGE can only be present when the value is text, which is useful for vague dates such as circa 1800.

The presence of a DEATHDATE property indicates that the subject of the vCard is known to be dead. Its absence makes no statement one way or the other.
sections.plainLanguage: If the death-date box is filled in, we know the person has died. If it is empty, it just means nobody wrote anything, not that the person is alive.

sections.title: Examples from the RFC
sections.content:
The examples show the three value styles: plain text, a URI to a description, and a geo: URI with coordinates. For dates they show a full date, a month and day with no year (--0415), and a free-text value.

One DEATHDATE example in the RFC text is printed as DEATHDATE;19531015T231000Z, without the VALUE= parameter name that the syntax would normally require. Treat the ABNF, not that line, as the rule.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show different ways to fill in the boxes: words, a link, map numbers, or a date.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The properties present no security considerations beyond those in Section 9 of the base vCard specification, RFC 6350. In short, nothing new is added to the risks of the format itself.
sections.plainLanguage: These boxes are no riskier than the boxes that were already on the contact card.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has added three entries to the vCard Properties registry, which is defined in Section 10.3.1 of RFC 6350. Each has an empty namespace and points back to this RFC: BIRTHPLACE to Section 2.1, DEATHPLACE to Section 2.2 and DEATHDATE to Section 2.3.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of contact-card boxes got three new lines so everyone uses the same names.

data.title: BIRTHPLACE, DEATHPLACE and DEATHDATE examples
data.code:
BIRTHPLACE:Babies'R'Us Hospital
BIRTHPLACE;VALUE=uri:geo:46.769307,-71.283079
DEATHPLACE:Aboard the Titanic\, near Newfoundland
DEATHPLACE;VALUE=uri:geo:41.731944,-49.945833
DEATHDATE:19960415
DEATHDATE:--0415
DEATHDATE;VALUE=text:circa 1800
